In [[field theory (mathematics)|field theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''Stufe''' ({{IPA|de|ˈʃtuːfə}}; German: "level") ''s''(''F'') of a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''F'' is the least number of squares that sum to −1. If −1 cannot be written as a sum of squares, ''s''(''F'') = <math>\infty</math>. In this case, ''F'' is a [[formally real field]].  [[Albrecht Pfister (mathematician)|Albrecht Pfister]] proved that the Stufe, if finite, is always a power of 2, and that conversely every power of 2 occurs.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=13}}

==Powers of 2==

If <math>s(F)\ne\infty</math> then <math>s(F)=2^k</math> for some [[natural number]] <math>k</math>.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=13}}{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=379}}

''Proof:'' Let <math>k \in \mathbb N</math> be chosen such that <math>2^k \leq s(F) < 2^{k+1}</math>. Let <math>n = 2^k</math>. Then there are <math>s = s(F)</math> elements <math>e_1, \ldots, e_s \in F\setminus\{0\}</math> such that

:<math>0 = \underbrace{1 + e_1^2 + \cdots + e_{n-1}^2 }_{=:\,a} + \underbrace{e_n^2 + \cdots + e_s^2}_{=:\,b}\;.</math>

Both <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are sums of <math>n</math> squares, and <math>a \ne 0</math>, since otherwise <math>s(F)< 2^k</math>, contrary to the assumption on <math>k</math>.

According to the theory of [[Pfister form]]s, the product <math>ab</math> is itself a sum of <math>n</math> squares, that is, <math>ab = c_1^2 + \cdots + c_n^2</math> for some <math>c_i \in F</math>. But since <math>a+b=0</math>, we also have <math>-a^2 = ab</math>, and hence

:<math>-1 = \frac{ab}{a^2} = \left(\frac{c_1}{a} \right)^2 + \cdots + \left(\frac{c_n}{a} \right)^2,</math>

and thus <math>s(F) = n = 2^k</math>.

==Positive characteristic==
Any field <math>F</math> with positive [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] has <math>s(F) \leq 2</math>.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=33}}

''Proof:'' Let <math>p = \operatorname{char}(F)</math>. It suffices to prove the claim for <math>\mathbb F_p</math>.

If <math>p = 2</math> then <math>-1 = 1 = 1^2</math>, so <math>s(F)=1</math>.

If <math>p>2</math> consider the set <math>S=\{x^2 : x \in \mathbb F_p\}</math> of squares. <math>S\setminus\{0\}</math> is a [[subgroup]] of [[Index of a subgroup|index]] <math>2</math> in the [[cyclic group]] <math>\mathbb F_p^\times</math> with <math>p-1</math> elements. Thus <math>S</math> contains exactly <math>\tfrac{p+1}2</math> elements, and so does <math>-1-S</math>.
Since <math>\mathbb F_p</math> only has <math>p</math> elements in total, <math>S</math> and <math>-1-S</math> cannot be [[disjoint sets|disjoint]], that is, there are <math>x,y\in\mathbb F_p</math> with <math>S\ni x^2=-1-y^2\in-1-S</math> and thus <math>-1=x^2+y^2</math>.

==Properties==
The Stufe ''s''(''F'') is related to the [[Pythagoras number]] ''p''(''F'') by ''p''(''F'') ≤  ''s''(''F'') + 1.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=44}}  If ''F'' is not formally real then ''s''(''F'') ≤ ''p''(''F'') ≤ ''s''(''F'') + 1.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=228}}{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=395}} The additive order of the form (1), and hence the [[Exponent of a group|exponent]] of the [[Witt group]] of ''F'' is equal to 2''s''(''F'').{{sfnp|Milnor|Husemoller|1973|p=75}}{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=380}}

==Examples==
* The Stufe of a [[quadratically closed field]] is 1.{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=380}}
* The Stufe of an [[algebraic number field]] is <math>\infty</math>, 1, 2 or 4 (Siegel's theorem).{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=381}}  Examples are <math>\Q</math>, <math>\Q(\sqrt{-1})</math>, <math>\Q(\sqrt{-2})</math> and <math>\Q(\sqrt{-7})</math>.{{sfnp|Milnor|Husemoller|1973|p=75}}
* The Stufe of a [[finite field]] <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math> is 1 if ''q'' ≡ 1 mod 4 and 2 if ''q'' ≡ 3 mod 4.{{sfnp|Rajwade|1993|p=33}}{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=380}}{{sfnp|Singh|1974}}
* The Stufe of a [[local field]] of odd residue characteristic is equal to that of its residue field.  The Stufe of the 2-adic field <math>\Q_2</math> is 4.{{sfnp|Lam|2005|p=381}}
